facts.summary: New York's minimum wage in 2026 is $17.00/hour in New York City, Long Island, and Westchester County, and $16.00/hour in the remainder of the state, well above the federal $7.25.
facts.citation: N.Y. Labor Law art. 19 (Minimum Wage Act); 12 NYCRR 142
facts.sourceAgency: New York State Department of Labor
facts.notes: Two-tier rate: $17.00 NYC/Long Island/Westchester, $16.00 rest of state, effective Jan 1, 2026. Starting 2027 the wage is indexed to inflation. Verify regional figure applicable to the worker's county.

facts.summary: New York's Human Rights Law bars employment discrimination on many bases beyond federal law, including sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, marital and familial status, military status, predisposing genetic characteristics, citizenship/immigration status, and domestic-violence-victim status.
facts.notes: List reflects Executive Law § 296(1)(a). Federal Title VII covers race, color, religion, sex, national origin; the ADEA covers age; NY adds the remaining categories listed here.

facts.summary: The New York Human Rights Law applies to all employers in the state regardless of size, unlike federal Title VII/ADA which require 15+ employees (ADEA 20+).
facts.notes: Section 292(5) defines 'employer' as 'all employers within the state.' The former four-or-more-employee threshold was eliminated by 2019 amendments (effective Feb 8, 2020).

facts.summary: A discrimination complaint may be filed with the New York State Division of Human Rights within three years of the most recent discriminatory act, longer than the EEOC's 180/300-day windows.
facts.sourceAgency: New York State Division of Human Rights (FEPA)
facts.notes: Three-year deadline applies to unlawful discriminatory acts occurring on or after Feb 15, 2024; for acts before that date only workplace sexual harassment retained a three-year window and other claims were subject to the prior one-year deadline. Verify which deadline applies to the specific act date.

facts.summary: An action to recover unpaid wages under the New York Labor Law must be commenced within six years, and back wages accrue for the entire six-year period.
facts.notes: Six-year statute of limitations is longer than the federal FLSA's two/three-year period.

facts.summary: New York's Human Rights Law makes it an unlawful discriminatory practice for an employer to refuse to provide reasonable accommodations to the known disabilities, or pregnancy-related conditions, of an employee, prospective employee, or member, unless the employer can demonstrate the accommodation would impose an undue hardship on its operations; retaliating against someone for requesting an accommodation is also unlawful.
facts.notes: Confirmed directly against the primary statute text (fetched from the official nysenate.gov consolidated-laws site): 296(3)(a) sets the accommodation duty and covers pregnancy-related conditions as well as disability; 296(3)(b) sets the undue-hardship exception (factors include size of the employer's business, budget, and nature/cost of the accommodation). Coverage follows Executive Law 292(5)'s 'all employers' definition (see discrimination.coverage, above) -- the older 4-employee threshold some secondary sources still cite predates the 2019 amendments (effective 2/8/2020) that eliminated it.

facts.summary: New York's whistleblower statute protects private employees from retaliation for disclosing, objecting to, or refusing to participate in activity they reasonably believe violates law or poses a substantial danger to public health or safety; suit must be brought within two years.
facts.notes: 2021 amendments broadened coverage (reasonable belief standard, former employees and independent contractors). Remedies include reinstatement, back pay, attorney's fees, and civil penalties up to $10,000. Public-sector employees are covered separately under Civil Service Law § 75-b.

facts.summary: For New York's executive and administrative overtime exemptions, employers in New York City, Nassau, Suffolk, and Westchester counties must pay at least $1,275.00/week ($66,300/yr) — well above the federal EAP salary floor of $684/week.
facts.sourceAgency: New York State Department of Labor
facts.notes: Effective Jan 1, 2026. Applies to the state executive and administrative exemptions only; New York sets no separate state salary threshold for the professional exemption, which continues to use the federal $684/week floor. The threshold rises annually — VERIFY 2027 figure when published. The primary PDF blocks automated fetch; figure cross-confirmed via multiple secondary legal-industry sources citing this NYSDOL wage order (12 NYCRR Part 142) before entry — re-verify against the primary source.

facts.summary: For New York's executive and administrative overtime exemptions, employers outside New York City, Nassau, Suffolk, and Westchester counties must pay at least $1,199.10/week ($62,353.20/yr) — above the federal EAP salary floor of $684/week.
facts.sourceAgency: New York State Department of Labor
facts.notes: Effective Jan 1, 2026. Applies to the state executive and administrative exemptions only; New York sets no separate state salary threshold for the professional exemption, which continues to use the federal $684/week floor. The threshold rises annually — VERIFY 2027 figure when published. facts.summary: New York has no comprehensive statutory ban on employee non-compete agreements (a 2023 bill to prohibit most non-competes was vetoed). Courts and the Attorney General apply a common-law reasonableness test: a non-compete is enforceable only to the extent it is no greater than necessary to protect the employer's legitimate interests, does not impose undue hardship on the employee, is not injurious to the public, and is reasonable in time period and geographic scope. Broadcast employers may not enforce non-competes against most on-air employees.
facts.citation: BDO Seidman v. Hirshberg, 93 N.Y.2d 382 (1999) (common-law standard); N.Y. Labor Law § 202-k (broadcast employees)
facts.notes: As of Jan 2026 the legislature is again considering a broader statutory ban (e.g. A10023/S4641-A, mirroring the bill Gov. Hochul vetoed in Dec 2023); no such ban is currently in effect. This entry may need revision if new legislation is enacted -- VERIFY periodically.

facts.value: by the regular payday for the pay period of termination
facts.summary: When employment ends, New York requires the employer to pay all wages owed no later than the regular payday for the pay period during which the termination occurred (by mail if the employee requests).
facts.notes: Federal law sets no final-pay deadline, so this is a New York addition. Section 191 also sets pay-frequency rules (e.g., weekly for manual workers).
